newsitem.title: RWANDA: Rwanda's Genocide Law defines guilt and punishment.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda's Genocide Law defines guilt and punishment.

text.p: The prisoners in pink shorts stooped over enamel bowls of steaming food, splitting potatoes and sifting through meat stew with their fingers until the soldiers were satisfied.
The guards at Rwanda's Gikondo prison were checking for weapons and other banned items at the thrice-weekly meal delivery by the families of some of the 5,000 inmates.
They are among 80,000 detainees, overwhelmingly from the Hutu majority, waiting to be charged, tried or released for their alleged role in the 1994 genocide in Rwanda.

The wheels of justice, to punish those who butchered up to one million people in a period of three months, have ground slowly. Rwanda's post-genocide government blames the delay on the murder or flight into exile of hundreds of judicial personnel and on the destruction of courts and files.
But early in September and with no fanfare the government adopted its Genocide Law, the crucial text for deciding levels of guilt and punishment in trials for years to come.
"We are making the last arrangements to start trials," said Gerard Gahima, the acting minister of justice.

The new law divides defendants into four categories but states that only those in category one are "liable to the death penalty". Execution will be by firing squad, Gahima told Reuters in an interview.

The law covers the period from October 1, 1990, to December 31, 1994. But the vast bulk of those who stand accused are blamed for their actions between April and June, 1994, when minority Tutsis and opposition supporters from the Hutu majority were targetted for extermination.

Category one is headed by those who planned, instigated and supervised the genocide or crimes against humanity. It includes prominent people, such as priests, who perpetrated or fostered genocide right down to village level. It covers killers who acted with "zeal and excessive malice" and people who may not have killed but who "committed acts of sexual torture".
Ordinary killers, the tens of thousands in the genocide's infantry, are in category two and liable to life imprisonment.
"You cannot punish everyone the same way or you would end up putting hundreds of thousands of people to death," Gahima said.
The transitional parliament broadened the scope of category one from the government's first draft.

The law contains a Confession and Guilty Plea procedure allowing reduced prison terms for those who confess honestly before trial. But even if they confess, people convicted in category one will not benefit from reduced penalties.
Category three is for serious assaults against the person and category four covers offences against property.
Gikondo's inmates want to know more about the Genocide Law. They have a sketchy knowledge of its provisions, gleaned from reports on Radio Rwanda.
"How does it fit in with the Penal Code?" Sylvestre Miseso, 28, secretary-general of the Gikondo prisoners' association, wanted to know from a visiting Reuters correspondent.

He said he was arrested in August 1995, 14 months after the end of the genocide, on the denunciation of someone who claimed he was manning a roadblock at Ruhengeri in April 1994. Tutsis and moderate Hutus were picked out at these roadblocks and usually put to death with machetes and clubs.

"I wasn't there, I was working in Kigali at the time. But I'm ready to be judged," said Miseso. He has a 'dossier', a legal file, and is accused of genocide. But he and other inmates thought as many as 50 percent of their number had no dossier and had not been charged.
An older man said he had been detained without charge since July, 1994. "None of us 94s have dossiers," he complained.
The group pressing around Miseso in Gikondo's central yard agreed about one thing. They had no intention of accepting the Confession and Guilty Plea offer.
"How can you confess to a crime you didn't commit? And nobody wants to ask for forgiveness without knowing what he's supposed to have done," Miseso said to general consent.

The paradox is that none of the genocide's big fish is in custody in Rwanda. They fled abroad in good time and now live in refugee camps in Zaire or Tanzania or in more comfortable exile in capitals around the world.
Those in the West, and in some African countries, are in little fear of extradition to Rwanda because courts oppose the existence of the death sentence.

The main threat to category one suspects abroad is that they will be extradited to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), the U.N. body created to try leaders of the genocide in Arusha, Tanzania.

But the ICTR, after nearly two years in existence and with a 1996 budget of $36 million, has so far managed to take only three suspects into its own custody. Unlike the 80,000 detainees in Rwanda, the trio's diet includes croissants for breakfast.
If they are hard-up, Arusha's suspects will have top defence lawyers paid for by the ICTR. If they are found guilty, life imprisonment in humane conditions will be the maximum penalty.
